sections.title: Progression Runs Spreadsheet Updates
sections.content: Matt reviewed and updated all progression runs with color coding for clarity and created two different weekly patterns to reduce available choices for users. Sandbox testing confirmed validation messages are working — no mileage inconsistencies found in current scenarios. Ben confirmed the system is designed to make these configuration changes trivial.

sections.title: Schedule Pattern Simplification
sections.content: Agreed to ask runners for their preferred long run day first, then offer two pattern options anchored to that day. If neither works, allow custom day selection with validation warnings. Three- and four-day runners might occasionally miss a moderate quality day due to spacing constraints, but five-plus day runners work in all scenarios.

sections.title: User Issue Categorization
sections.content: Defined three types of user issues: tweaks (short-term adjustments like an extra rest day), changes (tier-level reductions from accumulated fatigue), and seek help (stop running and see a doctor with cross-training until the user manually resumes). Need to determine how these overlay types interact when a race is approaching within one to two weeks.

sections.title: AI Knowledge Graph Vision
sections.content: Discussed building knowledge graphs from Matt's coaching expertise to power future AI responses. The system would use reinforcement learning to generate statistically-modeled responses, with low-confidence scenarios flagged back for human input. Not MVP — will be driven by patterns observed in early user feedback.

sections.title: Gap-Filling Logic
sections.content: Two types of infills for training plans. The starting infill bridges from onboarding to the first full training week, accounting for whether the runner ran today or yesterday. The ending infill aligns the two-week taper precisely with race day, filling any gap between the last full quality week and the taper start.

sections.title: Two-Week Taper Standard
sections.content: Confirmed a consistent two-week taper working backwards from race day. Last long run 14 days out can be serious. Quality workouts taper down through the final two weeks, with the last few days being easy with a shakeout before the race. Extended to three weeks only for runners with systemic health issues. Modern shoe technology has made two-week tapers effective even for lower-mileage runners.

sections.title: Schedule Pattern Design
sections.content: Instead of fully custom day selection, show two pre-built weekly patterns first. If neither works, offer custom selection with validation warnings for anti-patterns. Anti-patterns include three or more consecutive days off and four or more consecutive running days. Matt to write the warning messages in his coaching voice — authoritative but gentle.

sections.title: Pain Differentiation in Onboarding
sections.content: Added a follow-up question when a runner reports pain. Distinguishes between awareness of an issue (can run through it, seek help proactively, plan generates normally) versus pain that stops or limits running (defer plan, recommend medical consultation before starting, offer cross-training in the interim).

sections.title: Recovery by Race Distance
sections.content: After a 10K, two recovery days before the next stressor. After a half marathon, at least four recovery days. These rules affect how race overlays interact with the regular training schedule.

sections.title: Overlay Stacking Rules
sections.content: Ben expanded the I feel good / I'm tired / I'm in pain prompts into a weighted stacking system. When multiple conditions occur within a week, the response is based on the highest-weighted (most critical) condition. Added 'missed days due to life schedule' as a new scenario, plus race additions with different taper types based on race significance.

sections.title: Backend Testing Tool
sections.content: Demonstrated a tool for generating tier plans from any combination of onboarding inputs. Showed band assignments (start tier through end tier), build weeks, and taper placement. AI-driven testing of every input combination found edge cases — such as high-mileage runners on few days producing starting tiers lower than expected.

sections.title: Feedback Mechanism as Key Differentiator
sections.content: If a runner reports fatigue three consecutive times or five times within two weeks, their next workout becomes easy and they get a tier reduction. If the reduction happens twice in a build, keep them at their current level — the system has found their sweet spot. Agreed this feedback loop is what sets the product apart and warrants careful, thoughtful design. All rules will be configurable so they can be tuned after launch.

sections.title: Domain and App Distribution

sections.content: Shifted MVP target from August to January 1st. The complexity lies more in testing and infrastructure than in coding. This gives time for thorough testing, business planning, and marketing groundwork that hasn't started yet.

sections.title: Tier Assignment from Onboarding
sections.content: Using a 3-month average for determining typical running days and mileage rather than relying on what the runner did in the last couple weeks, which could be atypically low or high. Clear rules like miles per week and days per week determine the starting tier.

sections.title: Day Mapping and Optional Days
sections.content: Long runs and quality runs must be at least two days apart. Optional/bonus days fill remaining slots. The system needs deterministic assignment of these flex days while avoiding three or more consecutive days off. Some progression sheet discrepancies found where base runs didn't match between adjacent tiers.

sections.title: Onboarding Strategy
sections.content: Starting with conservative estimates and using the feedback mechanism to adjust upward. Focusing on the median runner rather than edge cases. Building a flexible system that gathers data to improve future iterations. Most runners will start at or near their current level.

sections.title: Mileage Range System
sections.content: Each day in the training plan gets separate low and high columns to show the mileage range. Using separate columns rather than hybrid values for simplicity. Formulas calculate weekly mileage ranges and long run percentages. Every meaningful user action will be captured for analytics.

sections.title: Training Transition Strategy
sections.content: Creating a gradual transition path for runners increasing from 4 to 5 to 6 days per week without losing built-up training. After three consecutive weeks at maximum mileage, the system prompts runners to either add a day or increase mileage — the intervention point that prevents stagnation.

sections.title: Onboarding Frequency Options

sections.title: Plan Duration and Truncation
sections.content: For half-marathon plans shorter than 13 weeks, the plan truncates from the end — keeping the early build weeks and replacing the last two with a taper based on peak mileage and running frequency. The assumption is that foundational workouts at the start of a build matter more than peak workouts for beginner to mid-tier runners.

sections.title: Plan Transition Guidelines
sections.content: When runners consistently hit the top of their range and regularly use optional days, those should become planned days — signaling readiness to graduate to the next plan tier. Need to separate questions about desired versus available running days during onboarding to handle this correctly.

sections.title: Rest Day Validation
sections.content: Soft gate of no more than two consecutive days off for 3-day-per-week runners. This is a strong coaching preference rather than an absolute rule. Stacking system differentiates fatigue responses based on race importance and distance categories.

sections.title: Business Model
sections.content: Annual subscriptions could provide flexibility for longer build-up periods in marathon training. Maintenance options between training cycles add value. Longer plans mean more revenue per customer and better training outcomes.

sections.title: Onboarding Questionnaire Design
sections.content: Minimal data collection for MVP: number of injuries in the last year costing a week or more, current weekly mileage, and runs per week. Postponing specific body part information. The overlay system handles ongoing feedback — onboarding just establishes the starting point.

sections.title: Check-In Categories
sections.content: Three categories replace numeric pain scales: Feel Great, Feel Tired, and In Pain. Each triggers specific overlay responses. The distinction between tired-with-discomfort and actual pain determines whether the system suggests rest or recommends medical consultation. These categories provide clearer guidance for users and deterministic triggers for the system.

sections.title: Injury-Based Tier Reduction
sections.content: Each distinct injury that cost a week or more of training in the last year results in a one-tier drop from the starting assignment. Age-based adjustments excluded from MVP due to complexity — running experience versus chronological age makes this hard to get right.

sections.title: Mileage Progression Approach
sections.content: Working backwards from desired peak levels is more effective than formula-based prediction. Matt to provide min/max mileage patterns for 3-7 day plans, showing concrete progressions rather than algorithmic calculations. The plan allows pacing increases rather than sudden jumps.

sections.title: Run Type Ratios
sections.content: Long run distance is the primary determinant for the entire week. Quality runs and weekly mileage ranges derive from it, with easy runs filling the remaining volume. One-mile-per-day increase approach up to five days per week. Users see previews of upcoming workouts but don't see actual mileage until they provide feedback — this prevents gaming the system.

sections.title: Intervention Mechanisms
sections.content: Need to define what happens when users report pain or miss workouts. Intervention scenarios will become coaching responses in the overlay system. Week-to-date mileage tracking helps runners understand their progress without chasing arbitrary weekly totals.
